summary: Explains how to build and read PKIX certificates used for SIP over TLS, in particular how to encode a SIP domain identity in a certificate and use it to authenticate a SIP domain. It is aimed at SIP implementers and certificate issuers. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A name badge for a phone-call server, so the other side can check it really belongs to the domain it claims.

questions: how to authenticate a sip domain
where does a sip certificate store the domain name
how does a sip client verify a tls server
subtitle: How a SIP server proves, with an X.509 certificate, that it speaks for a whole domain such as example.com.

tldr.problem: RFC 3261 says little about which certificate field carries a SIP domain's name, so implementations disagreed on how to authenticate a domain over TLS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says to put the SIP domain in the subjectAltName extension, spells out how to extract identities from a certificate, and gives exact matching rules (whole names only, no wildcards) for clients and servers.
tldr.outcome: SIP clients and servers get uniform domain authentication over TLS. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 3261.

facts.label: Fallback
facts.value: CN field, only if subjectAltName is absent

today: RFC 5922 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010. It updates RFC 3261 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Domain Certificates
sections.content:
SIP implementations increasingly use TLS (RFC 5246), and TLS authentication needs X.509 certificates as profiled in RFC 5280. But the existing SIP specification, RFC 3261, does not say enough about using certificates to authenticate a domain rather than a single host.

This RFC supplies conventions for building and reading certificates that identify their holder as authoritative for a SIP domain. It covers certificates used for a TLS connection only, not other uses such as S/MIME. It also updates RFC 3261.
sections.plainLanguage: When two phone-call servers talk, each wants proof of who the other is. This RFC says how to read that proof the same way everywhere.

sections.title: The Ambiguity in RFC 3261
sections.content:
For TLS, RFC 3261 (Section 26.3.1) only says that proxy servers, redirect servers and registrars SHOULD have a site certificate whose subject corresponds to their canonical hostname. It did not say where the identity goes: in the subjectAltName field, or as a Common Name (CN) in the Subject field. Legacy certificates often kept the identity in the CN.

It also did not say which identity to pick when a certificate holds several, or what to do when they use different schemes. TLS certificates bind the identities of the per-hop domains sending or receiving SIP messages, which differs from S/MIME certificates that are generally used end to end for a user.

For the passive side of a connection the old guidance is weaker still. RFC 3261 tells a server to compare the certificate's domain with the domain in the From header of the INVITE, but that domain is not always the one the request came from.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules did not say where on the name badge to write the name. Some people wrote it on the front, some on the back, so nobody could read them all the same way.

sections.title: From SIP Domain to Authenticated Server
sections.content:
A client takes the SIP URI it wants to reach (the Application Unique String, or AUS) and uses the RFC 3263 procedures to look up the domain in DNS. That yields addresses, ports and transports. If the transport is TLS, the client connects and the server presents its certificate in the handshake.

The client extracts identities from the certificate and compares them with the domain part of the original URI. If any one matches, the server is authenticated. For example, a request for sips:alice@example.com leads to a server whose certificate asserts sip:example.com, and the domain part matches.

The RFC notes that SIPS borrows this pattern from HTTPS (RFC 2818), but recommends a subjectAltName of type uniformResourceIdentifier rather than a dNSName. A name in a certificate is only a sequence of octets to compare; a valid certificate for example.com says nothing about subname.example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: You look up the address of the place you want to call, then ask the server at that address to show its badge. If the badge has the name you were looking for, you trust it.

sections.title: Mutual Authentication Between Proxies
sections.content:
In the SIP trapezoid, Alice's proxy at example.com connects to Bob's proxy at example.net, and each presents a certificate. The connecting proxy has an AUS to anchor its check. The proxy that accepts the connection passively does not, so it cannot simply compare against a target name.

For a passive server the RFC says the identity set taken from the client certificate can feed local policy. A very open policy validates the certificate and logs the identities. A stricter one keeps a list of domains it accepts connections from and checks each identity against it. If a client presents no certificate, it MUST NOT be considered authenticated, though whether to close the connection is a matter of local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: When two servers meet, both show badges. The one who was called has to decide for itself which badges it will accept, for example only from friends on its list.

sections.title: Finding and Comparing Identities
sections.content:
Implementations MUST first validate the certificate under RFC 5280 and check any extendedKeyUsage restrictions (RFC 5924 defines a SIP extended key usage). Then identities are found in this order:

  1. Examine each subjectAltName value. A URI with scheme sip and no userpart gives a SIP domain identity (its host part). A sip URI with a userpart (an @) MUST NOT be accepted, because it names a person. Other schemes are not accepted. A DNS name is accepted only if no sip URI identity is found.
  2. Only if subjectAltName is absent, an implementation MAY look at the CN and accept a valid DNS name there, for backward compatibility.

Comparison uses only the DNS name part, with no scheme or parameters, and is case insensitive (RFC 4343). Internationalized names follow Section 7.2 of RFC 5280. Names MUST match in their entirety: no suffix matching, so foo.example.com does not match example.com, and no wildcards, so *.example.com matches only the literal string *.example.com. This deliberately differs from HTTP over TLS, which allows wildcards.
sections.plainLanguage: Read the badge's special name line first, skip names that belong to one person, and compare the whole name letter for letter. A star on the badge is just a star, not a wildcard.

sections.title: What Each SIP Role Does
sections.content:
A client MUST compare the domain part of the AUS used for the RFC 3263 lookup against the identities from the server certificate. If no identities are found, or none match, the server is not authenticated and the client MUST close the connection immediately.

A proxy uses the client procedure when it opens a connection and the server procedure when it accepts one. A registrar and a redirect server follow the server behavior; a registrar can also challenge the client with HTTP Digest. A proxy that adds a Record-Route expecting secure connections MUST insert a URI matching an identity it holds a certificate for, or a secure connection to that URI will be impossible.

For virtual hosting, one certificate can list several domains in subjectAltName. If the TLS server_name extension (RFC 4366) is supported, the client SHOULD use it to request the certificate for the domain it wants.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever starts the call checks the badge and hangs up if it is wrong. Whoever answers can decide for itself which badges it likes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Used correctly, TLS with domain certificates gives confidentiality, integrity and authentication at each hop. The RFC expects, for example, that SIPS messages from Alice to Bob can be read only by the two users and by proxies holding domain certificates for their domains, and that Alice and Bob are transitively authenticated, assuming trust in the authoritative proxies.

The RFC also warns about using Digest authentication of one message to vouch for a whole connection or UDP peer. That goes beyond what Digest was designed to provide, so an implementation SHOULD NOT infer authentication of other messages that way. Domain authentication SHOULD instead be done with TLS and the certificate rules here.

Service providers are strongly encouraged to put identities in subjectAltName, which can hold several values, rather than the free-form Subject field.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking the badge at every handoff means a message cannot be read or changed along the way. Do not trust a whole conversation just because one message had a password.
